summary_html: Child safely **reunified with parent or guardian**, case closed. Federal policy treats reunification as the preferred outcome once risk factors are mitigated.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — establishes reunification timelines and permanency goals  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — funds reunification services and tracks permanency outcomes

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The Court reversed the court of appeals, holding that using the heightened clear-and-convincing standard at a permanency hearing is permissible and does not predetermine termination, and that the appellate court had improperly substituted its judgment for the juvenile court's.
key_cases.relevance: It explains that the permanency hearing asks only whether the child may safely be returned home, and that findings there do not dictate the later termination outcome.
key_cases.quote: When a foundation for the court's decision exists in the evidence, an appellate court may not engage in a reweighing of the evidence.

key_cases.holding: The Court held that Title II of the ADA applies to the provision of reunification services under Utah's child welfare statutes, but affirmed because the juvenile court acted within its discretion in finding the requested modifications to the reunification plan unreasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Reunification efforts that ignore a parent's disclosed disability may be legally inadequate, affecting whether reunification was genuinely attempted.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the ADA applies to the provision of reunification services

key_cases.holding: The Court retained deferential review of best-interest determinations but vacated in part because the juvenile court committed threshold legal errors in assessing whether the father had made sufficient progress in rehabilitation under the reunification statute.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a juvenile court must correctly assess a parent's statutory progress toward rehabilitation before it can lawfully conclude that reunification should give way to termination.
key_cases.quote: we reject the father's request that we abandon a deferential standard of review of a best interest determination

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that DCFS's individualized modifications to the mother's service plan for her learning disabilities, agoraphobia, and domestic-violence history satisfied both the reasonable-efforts requirement and Title II of the ADA.
key_cases.relevance: Reunification efforts must be tailored to a parent's disclosed disability for the resulting failure to reunify to be attributed to the parent.
key_cases.quote: Title II of the ADA prohibits public entities from discriminating against individuals with disabilities

key_cases.holding: The Court affirmed, holding that the juvenile court had subject matter jurisdiction because the mother voluntarily placed K.F. in state custody, that the order ending reunification and setting a goal of individualized permanency was final and appealable and appropriate where compelling reasons ruled out reunification, adoption, guardianship and kinship placement, and that the juvenile court's findings on service-plan compliance and on DCFS's reasonable efforts were owed broad discretion and were not clearly in error.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that whether reunification efforts were reasonable is a fact-intensive judgment for the juvenile court, and that a permanency goal may be moved off reunification when the parent has not complied with the service plan.
key_cases.quote: appellate courts defer to juvenile courts on matters of credibility, and juvenile courts have broad discretion in determining whether reasonable reunification efforts were made

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that the juvenile court is presumed to have applied the clear-and-convincing standard absent record evidence to the contrary, that the State made out a prima facie case of reasonable efforts, and that the court did not abuse its discretion in determining after trial that DCFS had made reasonable reunification efforts.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that friction with a caseworker and delay in starting family therapy did not make the reunification effort unreasonable, defining how much shortfall a parent must prove before the failure to reunify can be laid at the agency's door.
key_cases.quote: we discern no abuse of the juvenile court's discretion in its ultimate determination, made as factfinder after trial, that DCFS provided reasonable efforts toward reunification

search_keywords: Utah Division of Child and Family Services

state_agency.name: Utah Division of Child and Family Services

extended_foster_care_age: To age 21, only while the juvenile court orders DCFS to keep serving the young adult (Utah Code 80-1-102(56)(b)(i); 78A-6-120(1)(a)). A young adult who is 18 or older but younger than 21 and in DCFS custody on abuse, neglect, or dependency grounds may petition the juvenile court to be removed from division custody, and the court reviews that petition within 14 days; if removed, the young adult may petition within 90 days to re-enter division custody, and the juvenile court shall order the division to take custody (Utah Code 80-3-503)

common_failures: Failure to prove unfitness by clear and convincing evidence
Santosky v. Kramer standard not met

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Must file TPR or document compelling reason
